story:
The Cup in the Drawing

Bea was making Grandpa Len a surprise cup for his birthday on Saturday. She wanted it straight and smooth, just like the drawing. Then the shaping rib slipped and pressed a dent below the handle of the cup. Bea hid the dent behind the sponge. Bea said, “I could start again.” Mr Ivo said, “You can. But a new cup won't be ready for Saturday.” When Grandpa Len arrived, Bea brought out the cup, with its dent facing him. Bea said, “Your present has gone wrong. Will you help me?” Grandpa Len's stiff fingers would not curl around his old mug's narrow handle. Grandpa Len said, “My thumb needs somewhere here.” Bea said, “Where the dent is?” Bea said, “Then your present will be late. I want to make the handle bigger.” Bea flattened the wet cup. This time she shaped a handle big enough for his stiff fingers. On Saturday, Bea gave Grandpa Len only the drawing. He stood it beside his old mug. A week later, Bea brought the finished cup, fired and cool, to Grandpa Len's table. Grandpa Len took down the drawing and lifted the new cup by its broad handle. The old mug stayed on the shelf.

And that is where this story ends.

Nia wrote her name and Mateo's on the concert sheet. Beside them she drew two little drums. She wanted an answering beat at the concert. Nia tapped three quick beats. Mateo answered with two slow ones. Dalia opened the practice room door. Beyond it, chairs stood in rows. Mateo put his sticks down. Nia said, “What if it is just us, after the concert?” Mateo said, “With the door shut?” Nia said, “Shut.” Mateo picked up his sticks again. With the pencil, Nia struck out both names. Dalia gave their turn to the next child. After the last applause, Nia and Mateo moved their drums together in the practice room. Nia shut the practice room door. Nia tapped three quick beats. Two slow beats answered. On the concert sheet, both names lay beneath heavy pencil marks. Behind the closed door, neither drum was quiet for long.

Together they moved the flower beside the tray. Nia returned the empty can. Mr Bell hurried to the gate to meet the bus. At two, Nia was still turning the umbrella to follow the shade. The show had begun without her. The trolley stood unused. Under the umbrella, the yellow ribbon brushed the lifted seedling leaves.

Nia tied the yellow ribbon around the sunflower pot for the show at two. The show trolley waited by the door. In the greenhouse, the tomato seedlings drooped. One leaf had already curled. The broken tap gave no water. Mr Bell said, “One can left in the barrel. No repair part until tomorrow.” Mr Bell handed over the watering can. Nia filled it from the barrel. Mr Bell said, “The little class planted those.” Nia said, “Will half a can be enough?” Mr Bell said, “With shade. You must stay to keep moving the umbrella.” Mr Bell said, “Their bus is due. I must meet it at the gate.” Nia said, “I waited all year.” Nia watered her sunflower with the whole can. The tray got none. The torn shade cloth fell, leaving the tray in sunlight. Nia spent ten minutes packing the trolley, then looked back. Nia saw a leaf in the dry tray turn brown. Nia said, “I used all the water on mine.” Mr Bell said, “Help me shade what is still green.” Nia opened her umbrella above the tray. Its handle slid sideways. Nia said, “Hold it while I tie it.” Mr Bell steadied the handle with both hands. Nia tied the handle to the heavy pot. Together they moved the flower beside the tray. Nia returned the empty can. Mr Bell hurried to the gate to meet the bus. Nia stayed to adjust the shade. She missed the show. The leaf stayed brown. Nia pulled the umbrella over the remaining green leaves.

And that is where this story ends.
